note: 50 questions, all one level. Built for surprise while staying guessable. Every citation points at a source retrieved during research.

questions.prompt: How many children under 5 died in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 4.8 million children under five died — most from causes we already know how to prevent, like infection, birth complications and malnutrition.
questions.action: Look up the top three causes of death for young children.

questions.prompt: Malaria cases went which way between 2015 and 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: Malaria cases ROSE from 226 million to 263 million. It's one of the SDG measures moving backwards.
questions.action: Look up how malaria is transmitted and prevented.

questions.prompt: Since 2000, how many malaria deaths have been prevented worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: 12.7 million deaths averted, and 2.2 billion cases prevented. Even while cases rise, the fight against malaria has saved an extraordinary number of lives.
questions.action: Find out what a bed net costs and how many lives they've saved.

questions.prompt: How many women died in pregnancy or childbirth in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 260,000 women — roughly one every two minutes. Almost all of these deaths are preventable with skilled care.
questions.action: Work out how many that is per day.

questions.prompt: A woman in a low-income country is how much more likely to die giving birth than one in a high-income country?
questions.whyCorrect: 346 deaths per 100,000 births in low-income countries against 10 in high-income ones — roughly 35 times the risk, for the same biological event.
whyWrong: It's one of the widest health gaps in the world.
The gap is enormous, not small.
questions.action: Ask what makes childbirth safe — and what's missing where it isn't.

questions.prompt: In countries affected by conflict, the maternal death rate is:
questions.whyCorrect: 504 per 100,000 — more than two and a half times the global average of 197. War destroys the clinics and roads that make birth survivable.
whyWrong: That's close to the high-income figure.
questions.action: Ask what happens to a hospital during a war.

questions.prompt: How many people worldwide are living with HIV?
questions.whyCorrect: 40.8 million people. Thanks to treatment, most now live long lives — but 9.2 million still have no access to it.
questions.action: Look up how HIV treatment changed life expectancy.

questions.prompt: AIDS deaths fell from 1.4 million in 2010 to what in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 630,000 — cut by more than half in 14 years. One of the biggest public health successes in modern history.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — the toll is still enormous.
The fall was much steeper than this.
questions.action: Ask what made AIDS deaths fall so fast.

questions.prompt: How many people fell ill with tuberculosis in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 10.8 million new cases and 1.25 million deaths. TB is curable and still kills more people than almost any other infection.
questions.action: Look up how long TB treatment takes.

questions.prompt: How much did COVID-19 cut global life expectancy?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.8 years wiped off global life expectancy — reversing roughly a decade of progress in a single event.
whyWrong: It caused the largest drop in modern records.
questions.action: Ask an adult what changed in their life in 2020.

questions.prompt: How many health workers is the world short of?
questions.whyCorrect: A shortage of 14.7 million doctors, nurses and midwives — projected to still be 11.1 million by 2030.
questions.action: Find out how long it takes to train a nurse.

questions.prompt: How many people use tobacco worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.25 billion people. The good news: use has dropped by a third in two decades, with 118 million fewer users than in 2005.
questions.action: Look up how many deaths a year tobacco causes.

questions.prompt: How many people died by suicide in 2021?
questions.whyCorrect: 727,000 people. The rate has fallen from 12.5 to 9.2 per 100,000 since 2000, but it remains a leading cause of death among young people.
questions.action: Find out what mental health support exists at your school.

questions.prompt: Non-communicable diseases — heart disease, cancer, diabetes — killed how many people under 70 in 2021?
questions.whyCorrect: 18 million people died before 70 from diseases that aren't infectious. They're now the world's biggest killers, not epidemics.
questions.action: Name three habits that lower your risk of these diseases.

questions.prompt: What share of babies are born with a skilled health worker present?
questions.whyCorrect: 87%, up from 80% in 2015. That leaves roughly one birth in eight happening without trained help.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — coverage has improved a lot.
Too optimistic — millions of births still lack skilled care.
questions.action: Ask what a midwife actually does during a birth.

questions.prompt: How many people need treatment for neglected tropical diseases?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.495 billion people — down from 2.19 billion in 2010. These are diseases like river blindness that mostly affect the poorest.
questions.action: Look up one neglected tropical disease and who it affects.

questions.prompt: How many countries have eliminated at least one neglected tropical disease?
questions.whyCorrect: 54 countries by the end of 2024 — proof that diseases affecting the poorest can be beaten when there's focus and funding.
whyWrong: More countries than have achieved it.
questions.action: Find one country that eliminated a disease and how.

questions.prompt: How many countries are now certified malaria-free?
questions.whyCorrect: 44 countries and one territory. Malaria used to be common in Europe and North America — it was eliminated there, which shows it can be beaten.
whyWrong: Too many — malaria remains endemic in much of the world.
questions.action: Check whether malaria ever existed where you live.

questions.prompt: What share of children get the full three doses of the DTP vaccine?
questions.whyCorrect: 84% in 2023 — meaning roughly one child in six misses out on protection against diphtheria, tetanus and whooping cough.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — most children are vaccinated.
Too optimistic — global coverage has plateaued below this.
questions.action: Find out which vaccines you had as a baby.

questions.prompt: Aid for health nearly halved recently. From what to what?
questions.whyCorrect: From $22.1 billion to $13.4 billion in a single year — a sharp cut at a time when health systems were still recovering from COVID.
questions.action: Ask what a health system loses when funding drops suddenly.

questions.prompt: Child deaths under 5 fell from 44 per 1,000 births in 2015 to what in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 37 per 1,000 — real progress, though still meaning 4.8 million children died in a single year.
whyWrong: Child mortality fell rather than rose.
Too optimistic — that's closer to wealthy-country rates.
questions.action: Notice that progress and tragedy can be true at once.

questions.prompt: Newborn deaths — babies dying in their first month — are what share of under-5 deaths?
questions.whyCorrect: At 17 per 1,000 out of 37 total, newborn deaths are nearly half of all under-5 deaths. The first month of life is by far the most dangerous.
whyWrong: Far too low — the newborn period dominates child mortality.
questions.action: Ask why the first 28 days are so risky.

questions.prompt: How many teenage girls gave birth in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 12.4 million births to mothers aged 15–19 — down from 13.9 million in 2015, but still enormous.
questions.action: Look up how early pregnancy affects a girl's schooling.

questions.prompt: How much did healthy life expectancy improve between 2000 and 2019?
questions.whyCorrect: More than five extra years of healthy life in under two decades — then COVID took 1.8 of them back.
whyWrong: The gain was around ten times larger.
It rose substantially before the pandemic.
questions.action: Ask what improvements added those five years.

questions.prompt: How many people with HIV still have no access to treatment?
questions.whyCorrect: 9.2 million people. Treatment exists, works, and keeps people alive — they simply can't get it.
questions.action: Ask what stops a working medicine from reaching people.

questions.prompt: How many children are living with HIV?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.4 million children. Most were infected around birth — which is preventable when mothers get treatment.
questions.action: Look up how mother-to-child HIV transmission is prevented.

questions.prompt: Alcohol consumption per person has moved which way since 2010?
questions.whyCorrect: Down from 5.7 to 5.0 litres of pure alcohol per person per year. Around 56% of adults don't drink at all.
questions.action: Look up how alcohol affects a developing brain.

questions.prompt: Tobacco use has fallen by roughly how much in two decades?
questions.whyCorrect: Down by about a third, with 118 million fewer users than in 2005 — one of the great public health wins, driven by taxes, bans and warnings.
questions.action: Find out what your country did to reduce smoking.

questions.prompt: The global health workforce is about how large?
questions.whyCorrect: About 70 million health workers — and still 14.7 million short of what's needed.
questions.action: Count how many health workers you've met in your life.

questions.prompt: Maternal deaths fell from 228 per 100,000 births in 2015 to what in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: 197 per 100,000 — progress, but far too slow to reach the 2030 target of under 70.
whyWrong: Too optimistic — progress has been slower than this.
Maternal mortality fell rather than rose.
questions.action: Work out how far 197 is from the target of 70.

questions.prompt: Which kills more people each year: tuberculosis or AIDS?
questions.whyCorrect: TB killed 1.25 million people in 2023 against 630,000 AIDS deaths in 2024 — about twice as many, from a disease that's curable with antibiotics.
whyWrong: TB kills roughly twice as many.
AIDS deaths have more than halved since 2010.
questions.action: Ask why a curable disease still kills over a million people.

questions.prompt: What share of married women can make their own decisions about their reproductive health?
questions.whyCorrect: Only 56.3% — meaning nearly half of married women can't fully decide about contraception or their own healthcare.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic, though the real figure is troubling.
questions.action: Ask what 'full decision-making power' should mean.

questions.prompt: The risk of dying early from non-communicable disease has moved which way since 2000?
questions.whyCorrect: Down from 22.5% to 18% — but progress stalled after 2015, and these diseases still kill 18 million people under 70 every year.
whyWrong: The risk fell rather than rose.
There was a clear improvement, then a plateau.
questions.action: Name the four main non-communicable diseases.

questions.prompt: Since 2000, how many malaria cases have been prevented?
questions.whyCorrect: 2.2 billion cases prevented — more than a quarter of everyone alive today, spared an illness that might have killed them.
questions.action: Ask which tools prevented those 2.2 billion cases.

questions.prompt: Least developed countries received what share of health aid in 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: $5.5 billion of $13.4 billion — about 40% went to the least developed countries, where health needs are greatest.
whyWrong: Too high — most aid is spread more widely.
questions.action: Ask whether aid should go where need is greatest.

questions.prompt: The suicide rate has moved which way since 2000?
questions.whyCorrect: Down from 12.5 to 9.2 per 100,000. Real progress — and it still means 727,000 deaths a year.
whyWrong: The rate fell rather than rose.
questions.action: Find out who someone can talk to if they're struggling.

questions.prompt: TB rates are falling, but by how much between 2015 and 2023?
questions.whyCorrect: Just 8.3% in eight years — far too slow. At this pace TB will still be killing over a million people a year for decades.
whyWrong: Progress has been much slower than this.
questions.action: Ask what would speed up progress on TB.

questions.prompt: Which age group is most at risk of dying in childhood?
questions.whyCorrect: The first month of life. Newborn deaths are 17 of the 37 per 1,000 under-5 deaths — nearly half.
whyWrong: This is the safest of the three.
Risk drops sharply after the newborn period.
questions.action: Ask what care a newborn needs in the first 48 hours.

questions.prompt: The health worker shortage is projected to be what by 2030?
questions.whyCorrect: 11.1 million — improving from today's 14.7 million, but still an enormous gap at the SDG deadline.
whyWrong: The gap narrows but doesn't close.
Too high — the shortage is projected to shrink.
questions.action: Ask what would make more people train as nurses.

questions.prompt: Adolescent birth rates fell from 45.9 per 1,000 in 2015 to what in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 38.3 per 1,000 — a meaningful drop, closely linked to girls staying in school longer.
whyWrong: The rate fell rather than rose.
Too optimistic — the decline was steady, not dramatic.
questions.action: Ask how staying in school affects when someone starts a family.

questions.prompt: How many new HIV infections were there in 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 1.3 million new infections. Despite treatment successes, prevention is still falling well short.
questions.action: Ask why treatment progress outpaced prevention.

questions.prompt: Modern contraceptive use has barely moved since 2015. What is it now?
questions.whyCorrect: 77.2%, up from just 76.4% in 2015 — almost no change in a decade, leaving millions unable to plan their families.
whyWrong: Too pessimistic — coverage is above three-quarters.
Too optimistic — nearly a quarter still lack access.
questions.action: Ask what stops someone accessing family planning.

questions.prompt: Which region has the highest maternal death rate?
questions.whyCorrect: Low-income countries at 346 per 100,000, against 10 in high-income countries — a 35-fold gap.
whyWrong: High-income countries have the lowest rate at 10.
One of the widest gaps in global health.
questions.action: Ask what a hospital needs to make birth safe.

questions.prompt: Neglected tropical diseases affected 2.19 billion people in 2010. What about now?
questions.whyCorrect: About 1.495 billion — nearly 700 million fewer people needing treatment. Enormous progress on diseases that get almost no attention.
whyWrong: The number fell substantially rather than rising.
Too optimistic — over a billion people are still affected.
questions.action: Ask why these diseases are called 'neglected'.

questions.prompt: Malaria's incidence rate in 2023 was about:
questions.whyCorrect: 60.4 cases per 1,000 people at risk — meaning roughly 1 in 17 people living in malaria zones catch it each year.
whyWrong: That would be more than half of everyone at risk.
questions.action: Work out what 60 per 1,000 means as a fraction.

questions.prompt: What's the biggest killer of people under 70 worldwide?
questions.whyCorrect: Non-communicable diseases — heart disease, cancer, diabetes and lung disease — killed 18 million people under 70 in 2021. The world's disease burden has shifted.
whyWrong: Infections still kill millions, but NCDs now dominate.
Accidents are a serious cause but far smaller.
questions.action: Name the four main non-communicable diseases.

questions.prompt: How many people avoid alcohol entirely?
questions.whyCorrect: About 56% of people aged 15 and over don't drink at all — the majority of the world, which surprises most people.
whyWrong: Far too low — most adults worldwide don't drink.
Too high, though abstainers are the majority.
questions.action: Ask whether that number matches what you'd assumed.

questions.prompt: Skilled birth attendance rose from 80% in 2015 to what by 2024?
questions.whyCorrect: 87% — seven percentage points in nine years, meaning millions more women giving birth with trained help.
whyWrong: The improvement was larger than this.
Too optimistic — around one birth in eight still lacks skilled care.
questions.action: Ask what difference a trained attendant makes at a birth.

questions.prompt: Health aid dropped sharply in 2023. Why does timing matter?
options: It fell while systems were still recovering from COVID
Aid was replaced by something better
questions.whyCorrect: Funding fell from $22.1bn to $13.4bn just as countries were rebuilding after the pandemic and facing rising malaria and TB.
whyWrong: Malaria cases rose and 14.7 million health workers are still missing.
No replacement source made up the gap.
questions.action: Ask what a clinic cuts first when its budget falls.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the clearest good-news story in global health?
options: AIDS deaths more than halved since 2010
questions.whyCorrect: AIDS deaths fell from 1.4 million to 630,000 — one of the great successes. Malaria cases actually rose, and health aid fell sharply.
whyWrong: Health aid nearly halved between 2022 and 2023.
questions.action: Ask what made the AIDS response work where others stalled.
